newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade protestors ignore beatings, snow.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade protestors ignore beatings, snow.

text.p: Undaunted by police beatings and severe winter weather, scores of thousands of opponents of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic protested in Belgrade on Wednesday to demand recognition of local election results.

Despite falling snow and frigid temperatures, demonstrators marched peacfully through the city after seething street battles on Tuesday when surging pro- and anti-Milosevic crowds clashed and police waded in to separate the factions.
Wednesday was the 36th successive day of what have become ritual protests with carnival-like overtones.
Blowing whistles and trumpets and chanting anti-Milosevic slogans, the marchers snaked through central Belgrade, drawing waves and cheers of support from onlookers.
Snowballs and firecrackers were thrown along the route but there was no repeat of Tuesday's violence or massive police presence.
One local radio station put the size of the anti-government crowd at 100,000 people, about half the number the Zajedno (Together) coalition fielded the day before.

The demonstrations first erupted after Milosevic and the ruling SPS party used its lock on government power to overturn opposition victories in municipal elections on November 17 in several cities and towns, including Belgrade.
For more than a month, the daily protests passed off without serious incident, but the SPS brought supporters into Belgrade on Tuesday for a rally at the same time and place as the opposition.

Opposition leaders denounced the move as a blatant provocation and Belgrade's emergency medical centre treated 58 people for injuries in the ensuing clashes. One man was in critical condition after being shot in the head by an SPS supporter.
Vuk Draskovic, leader of the opposition Serbian Renewal Movement, said the clashes had let the genie of violence out of the bottle and marked "the beginning of civil war in Belgrade."

Zoran Djindjic, leader of the opposition Democratic Party, said that "the Serbian authorities have totally lost their compass" and Milosevic might be preparing to try to block further street protests.

"We have information that Mr. Milosevic yesterday reached a decision to ban rallying and that the state services are now getting ready to implement it," Djindiic told reporters, vowing that the opposition would defy any ban on marches.

The United States and France said they held Milosevic responsible for Belgrade's street violence and German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said any further violence would damage Yugoslav efforts to reintegrate with Europe.

Western governments spent much of the last year praising Milosevic as a responsible world leader for his work in support of the Bosnian peace agreement but are now distancing themselves from Europe's last communist dictator.

A fact-finding mission by the trans-Atlantic Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) is expected to deliver its view within the week of the November 17 elections and of the tense political situation inside Serbia.
The Russian Foreign Ministry called on the Serbian people to avoid actions which could lead to further violence.
But in wording clearly aimed at the West the statement said outside interference in the internal affairs of the Serbian people was "inadmissable".

Milosevic is apparently counting on Moscow to block any effort by the U.N. Security Council to pressure him by reimposing the economic sanctions lifted earlier this year in the wake of the Bosnia peace deal.
